Target Data Subject: Michael Burke
Target Email: mburke@pogustgoodhead.com
Aliases: MB, Michael, Michael B., M. Burke

INSTRUCTIONS:
1. TARGETED THREAD ANALYSIS: Focus your analysis primarily on the MOST RECENT (top-level) email AND the IMMEDIATELY FORWARDED/REPLIED-TO email (the second email in the chain).
2. "KEEP" DECISION: You MUST return "keep" ONLY IF the Data Subject:
   - Is a Sender, Recipient, CC, or BCC of the top-level email OR the immediately forwarded/replied-to email.
   - Is explicitly discussed or mentioned by name in the newly written body text of the top-level email.

   - Case Study: John (Subject) sends an email to Jane. Jane forwards John's email to Pedro. Pedro replies to Jane adding Sandra.
   - Analysis: In this scenario, keep the original message John sent to Jane, and the email Jane forwarded to Pedro (as it contains the direct communication from the Subject). Discard subsequent emails where the Subject's message is no longer actively discussed.

   - Case Study: Anne sends an email to Bob. Anne's email contains an attached email from the Subject to Carlos.
   - Analysis: Keep the attached email because the Subject is a participant. Keep Anne's email because it is the physical carrier of the attachment and must be preserved to allow extraction.
6. OUTPUT FORMAT: You must return ONLY a raw JSON object. Do not wrap the output in markdown code blocks (```json). Do not add conversational text.
Format exactly like this: {"decision": "keep" | "discard", "reason": "Brief justification."}

{"emailHash":"1b3b3da0331135b5f87d984c8a71d13b763f03d9d22b36f65ecdf15e874e2aa8","parentHash":null,"sequentialName":"Email 4818","from":"Raminder Grewal","to":"Oliver Shipway; Anna Varga; Greg Lewis; Erika Saluzzo","subject":"Re: proposed handover","date":"2025-11-25T11:22:23.000Z","attachments":true,"body":"\r\n\r\nThanks Oliver - the handover protocol and client comms process is attached FYI. R​​​​Raminder GrewalGlobal HR Director+44 (0) 7890 043 718From: Oliver Shipway <oshipway@pogustgoodhead.com>Date: Tuesday, 25 November 2025 at 11:14To: Raminder Grewal <rgrewal@pogustgoodhead.com>, Anna Varga <avarga@pogustgoodhead.com>, Greg Lewis <glewis@pogustgoodhead.com>, Erika Saluzzo <esaluzzo@pogustgoodhead.com>Cc: Natasha Geraldo Baird <ngeraldobaird@pogustgoodhead.com>Subject: Re: proposed handoverThanks Raninder. I haven't seen the handover protocol and this is probably covered but re Matt, the value in the handover note is in pointing to the available resources to understand the case and how it is run (including who is who), providing or referring to summary information to get up the curve   (eg instructions to counsel or otherwise) and giving any critical details that are only in the case leads head. Sent from Outlook for iOS​​​​Oliver ShipwayPartnerFrom: Raminder Grewal <rgrewal@pogustgoodhead.com>Sent: Tuesday, November 25, 2025 10:59:56 AMTo: Anna Varga <avarga@pogustgoodhead.com>; Greg Lewis <glewis@pogustgoodhead.com>; Erika Saluzzo <esaluzzo@pogustgoodhead.com>; Oliver Shipway <oshipway@pogustgoodhead.com>Cc: Natasha Geraldo Baird <ngeraldobaird@pogustgoodhead.com>Subject: Re: proposed handover Good morning all, I wanted to share a brief update on where we’ve got to with the outgoing CL handovers: (spoiler: not very far unfortunately, as they have been busy with trial so we will need to ramp up the pressure as this is obviously a key priority prior to their exit)Matt: He has indicated to me that he is drafting a handover note (but refuses to use the handover protocol template). His comment is copied below fyi. I have emailed him this morning to confirm that, in the best interests of the Clients, we do need a full and detailed handover and to ask for an ETA on the note, as well as his availability for a handover meeting.Please let me know who will be taking over as the CL for Matt’s work so we can set up the meeting. "There isn't really any substitute for just reading the documents, so whenever the next PCD caselead is chosen they should spend as much time as possible reading as much as possible.  There is plenty to get started with that is not confidential: GPOC, IPOCs, the GLO, all pan-NOx orders and judgments, the PDD trial skeleton arguments.  Those documents are all already in a folder available for third parties.  Anyone in the emission department can grant the next caselead access when we know who they are".Michael: He has taken leave this week, as you may be aware. I have emailed to advise him that he needs to complete the handover as soon as he returns and asked for his availability to meet with @Greg Lewis to conduct a f2f handover too. Priyanka: She has yet to complete the handover and I have chased for this, as well as requesting availability for a handover meeting - please let me know who will be the incoming workstream lead. Georgina:  Georgina did revert to me regarding the handover and commented as follows: "My only real question is when I am to be expected to complete this. I am in full trial prep mode, have 2 cases to complete running back to back and am already working every evening and weekend. I am also extending past my end date to assist the firm and to conclude one of my cases". Please let me know how you would like us to manage this, as I appreciate the difficulty given her trial runs right up to her exit date.Thanks, R​​​​Raminder GrewalGlobal HR Director+44 (0) 7890 043 718From: Anna Varga <avarga@pogustgoodhead.com>Date: Monday, 24 November 2025 at 09:55To: Raminder Grewal <rgrewal@pogustgoodhead.com>Cc: Greg Lewis <glewis@pogustgoodhead.com>, Erika Saluzzo <esaluzzo@pogustgoodhead.com>, Oliver Shipway <oshipway@pogustgoodhead.com>Subject: Re: proposed handoverHi RaminderDid you respond to MB? Keen that we push him to do it this week. Also we should remind Matt that he needs to do his h/over note.A​​​​Anna VargaPartner+44 (0) 7890 043 699From: Raminder Grewal <rgrewal@pogustgoodhead.com>Sent: Friday, November 21, 2025 3:14 PMTo: Anna Varga <avarga@pogustgoodhead.com>Subject: FW: proposed handoverFYI​​​​Raminder GrewalGlobal HR Director+44 (0) 7890 043 718From: Michael Burke <mburke@pogustgoodhead.com>Date: Friday, 21 November 2025 at 14:47To: Raminder Grewal <rgrewal@pogustgoodhead.com>Subject: Re: proposed handoverDear Raminder,Thank you for your email. I am on leave today (although I have been assisting the team in completing another deadline), however in light of the below, and to aid in my recovery after such an intense period of work, I will also appreciate taking the next week off to attempt to recover and recuperate, such that I am fit for work.I have requested this on HiBOB, thank you. Thanks,Michael​​​​Michael Burke(He/Him)Partner+44 (0) 7960 032 34407960 032 344From: Raminder Grewal <rgrewal@pogustgoodhead.com>Sent: 18 November 2025 6:00 PMTo: Michael Burke <mburke@pogustgoodhead.com>Subject: Re: proposed handover Dear Michael, Thank you for coming back to me about the handover. It’s completely understandable that your focus has been entirely on the trial, and I hope it all went smoothly.Now that the trial has concluded, it would be most helpful if you could turn your attention to the handover. Anna Varga has suggested to me that you may appreciate taking a day or two off in between to decompress after such an intense period, so please feel free to do so if you wish and let Anna know. I know we’ve discussed the option of you leaving the firm earlier than your notice period, and if that’s still what you’d prefer, you’re welcome to do so once the handover has been completed and signed off by Anna. Many thanks, Raminder​​​​Raminder GrewalGlobal HR Director+44 (0) 7890 043 718From: Michael Burke <mburke@pogustgoodhead.com>Date: Monday, 10 November 2025 at 19:46To: Raminder Grewal <rgrewal@pogustgoodhead.com>Subject: proposed handoverHi Raminder, Thanks for your Teams message (15.23) regarding the handover protocol, attached, just so it is all in one place.I have not considered the document yet and will be unable to do so until Ford finishes in trial. As you will be aware, including from my email of 9 November, Ford started in trial today and it requires 100% of my attention from now until completion. To focus on tasks not trial related will require me to not concentrate fully on the trial.As such, and as informed in my 9 November email, I am unable to complete a handover when in trial. The earliest I will be able to consider this will be 19 November. Thanks,Michael​​​​Michael Burke(He/Him)Partner+44 (0) 7960 032 34407960 032 344"}

Dear Raminder,


Thank you for coming back to me and for accepting my resignation. My apologies for the delay in coming back to you, as I’m sure
 you are aware there are a lot of things in the air!


Noting your comments regarding my resignation being premature, I disagree with that assessment, but we are where we are. What is
 important is that we find a way to move forward that ensures the clients of Pogust Goodhead (and other firms) are not prejudiced or detrimentally impacted moving forward and that we are all content with. I trust that my conduct since submitting my notice demonstrates
 that I am committed to working with the firm to progress this in a professional and orderly fashion. This email has some detail in it so if it is easier for us to hop on a call to try and cut through bits of it or to have a quicker conversation, I'm more than
 happy to do so. 


This email is in two parts: i) to address my notice period and when may be a good time for me to depart the firm; and ii) to address
 on-going travel and litigation needs with a view to finding a pragmatic way to handle future travel etc.


Notice Period


I agree that we need to work collaboratively to find an appropriate point for me to leave the firm, both to ensure the clients
 are protected and not disadvantaged, and to ensure that I am protected and not prejudiced. My current leave date is I understand the 15 December 2025. There are various important deadlines between now and then an to add a little more colour to those deadlines,
 the deadlines we have approaching (demarcated as PDD or Quantum) are as follows:



06.10.2025 – PTR 2 (PDD)
10.10.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
13.10.2025 – Trial starts (PDD)
21.11.2025 – Individual Particulars of Quantum to be filed and served (Quantum)
11.12.2025 – receipt of disclosure from Defendants (Quantum)
19.12.2025 – Trial ends (PDD)



19.12.2025 – Applications for January 2026 CMC (Quantum)




As is evident, the litigation has a large number of critical deadlines looming. Overlayed with this, is the added complication of each OEM having its own CRO, as well as an overall Pan-NOx
 CRO.


Each individual must apply to the Defendants (individually per CRO and to all Defendants for the Pan-Lead CRO) for permission to
 be entered into that CRO. This takes up to 5 working days. There is also a process for applying to be removed from each CRO which can, in itself, take some days.


Given the level of confidential information in the NOx litigations, someone who is not in one, or all, of the CROs, is necessarily
 extremely limited as to what they can see, do and work on. For example, they could not actively participate in the trial, nor could they provide any type of meaningful input into any of the directions that fall across the period that they are not in the CRO
 i.e. the IPQs. If therefore I am held to work my notice until 15 December, I will be unable to attend trial for the final week before Christmas, nor will I will be able to really assist with any work on quantum disclosure, or work on the applications / witness
 statements for the January 2026 CMC.


Considering this, we (both me and Pogust Goodhead) need to realistically consider when my departure should fall, as it should come
 at a time that will be at the least detriment of the claimants.


To that end, it seems sensible, and would be in everyone’s interests, for me to depart Pogust Goodhead on a date that will allow
 me to start my new role and be re-entered into the various CROs, which does not conflict with any of those deadlines, nor run over a critical part of the trial that I am intended to participate in. To require me to serve my notice such that I leave the firm
 on a date which conflicts with a major deadline would be of significant detriment to the clients, not only of this firm, but to other firms as well.


Having considered the timetable and what is genuinely in the best interests of everyone, especially the clients, it would appear
 the best date for me to depart Pogust Goodhead is the 17 October. This date falls after the opening submissions, and across the Normal Driving Conditions expert evidence (which is plainly of importance, but falls at the lower end of the scale of importance
 considering the other critical tasks over the trial period). Exiting Pogust Goodhead then, will allow me sufficient time to commence my new role before substantive evidence relating to the manufacturers starts.


Any other date past this, will cause significant issues with my involvement over key aspects of the trial and, I believe, will
 have a negative impact on the claimants. For a Partner with current conduct of an ALGLO, who has detailed knowledge of all of the cases across the Pan-NOx Litigation, to be unable to participate in the trial, is not in anyone’s interests. The obvious link
 is that any prohibition on me being able to work on these cases, also directly impacts the Pogust Goodhead claimants and the prospects of their claims being successfully concluded.


Without wishing this to become a confrontational or protracted process (as I am committed to progressing this in a professional
 and orderly fashion), if Pogust Goodhead wish me to remain in post past this date, I would ask that they provide good reason why, including an explanation of why they do not believe this will impact the clients (including why they believe it is in the clients
 best interests) including the trial timetable and the quantum deadlines.


I would ask this be provided to assist me with any future queries that may be raised of me in respect of compliance with my professional
 and regulatory obligations i.e. "why did you leave during the PDD Trial or  why didn't you leave at a point when you would be restricted from working on critical quantum workstreams?".


Future Travel


While we resolve the issue of my notice period, I am conscious that it is “business as usual” and I am committed to this. As such,
 I will be needing to continue to travel to London for work in the office and for attendance at trial (while I am still employed by the firm).


I appreciate the arrangement I have with the firm is that they will book my flights for me. Given I wish to make bookings into
 the future, past the date which I have given above as my preferred leave date, I would suggest that it is more pragmatic, to ensure they the firm is not put to more expense than is needed, for me to take charge of booking my flights, which I can then claim
 back through expenses. Going forward then, flights which occur over the dates of my employment, I would seek to recover in expenses. For any flights booked that occur past my leave date, I would then cover the cost of myself (as I would no longer be in the
 employ of the firm).


This strikes me as inherently more sensible than continuing to have the firm book my flights, as in an instance where the firm
 has booked a flight for me which is due to take off after my leave date, I would not be able to travel on that flight, and I would need to re-book the flight most likely at a higher price.


Additional to this (and at a higher cost), is the flat that the firm has rented for me the duration of the trial. This rental starts
 on 6 October and runs until 21 December. I am intending on using this for as long as I am with the firm. The firm however, especially if they are agreeable to my suggested leave date, may wish to consider cancelling this booking and instead booking me into
 hotels until my leave date. This may be something that the firm considered a more pragmatic and financially sound option. I am comfortable either way and am happy to have an open dialogue on how best to manage this.


Until hearing otherwise, I will change my flight booking system such that I will make flight bookings personally and the recover
 the cost via expenses, and I will proceed as if to stay in that flat over the remainder of my employment.


I look forward to hearing from you, and should you require anything further, please let me know.


Best,


Michael

Dear Board,




We write further to the emails exchanged between Michael Burke, Sarah Bingham and Anna Varga dated 15 and 16 October 2025 as they relate to the Litigation Management Agreement ("LMA") and Agency Agreement ("AA"). This email is intended
 to be a protected disclosure. 




As can be seen from the First Witness Statement of Alicia Alinia dated 30 September at paragraph 35.1 - she has confirmed (and verified with a statement of truth): "For the avoidance of doubt, Gramercy has no control over the day-to-day management or decisions
 of the Firm or the Partner, and nor does Gramercy have any role in the conduct, control or management of the NOx Group Litigations."




Further, at 35.3, it is confirmed that "Its board of directors is entirely independent of Gramercy, and nothing in its financial arrangements inhibits the Firm from actively, and independently, pursuing the Proceedings in the best interests of its clients."




On account of the email sent by Anna Varga on 16 October at 8.57AM in which she explicitly instructs Sarah Bingham to instruct Stewarts (who are retained by Gramercy - see email from Joshua Katz dated 13.05.2025 confirming this) to provide input into documents
 central to the NOx Litigation - the statement at 35.1 is now categorically untrue. Senior management has instructed a member of staff to engage with a firm which is instructed by Gramercy to review both Pan NOx and PG specific documents. This position therefore
 must be corrected to the Court and to the Defendants (and to the PG staff) where the firm have represented that Gramercy does not have input into the conduct of the Litigations (in the case of to the Court - with a signed statement of truth). 




With regard to 35.3 - see the email from Julian Chamberlayne on 9 September 2025 at 11.30 in which he confirms that "I have now heard from Gramercy that, based on our review, they are content with you proceeding with the revised agency agreements" .
 In circumstances where Stewarts, instructed by Gramercy, are reviewing and providing approval in respect of key NOx documents and requiring PG to await execution prior to their approval, it cannot be true to state that the Firm can independently pursue the
 Proceedings (and is in fact doing so) cannot be true. 

We completely understand that a litigation funder will have a legitimate interest in reviewing certain documents, and may quite properly wish to have input where those documents either (a) give rise to a financial liability on the funder, or (b) relate to compliance
 with the funding terms.

We also acknowledge PG’s position under the funding arrangements in particular, the covenant requiring PG to obtain the funder’s prior approval before engaging any new law firm or barrister to whom PG grants a contingent interest. This requirement exists because
 such engagements could create a financial exposure that Gramercy may ultimately need to meet.

However, the Pan-NOx Agency Agreement does not fall within that category. It does not create any contingent interests, nor does it involve any cost contribution obligations from the Non-Lead Firms. Its purpose is purely to define the principal–agent relationship between
 Pogust Goodhead (as Lead Solicitor) and the Non-Lead Firms, governing the conduct, management, strategy decisions and coordination of the litigation. In short, it enables PG to act independently as Lead Solicitor within the proceedings.

Similarly, the Litigation Management Agreement is not a funding or liability document. Rather, it is an agreement between the Client Committee and Pogust Goodhead, setting out the instructions, authority and governance framework under which PG acts for the
 claimants within each GLO. It defines procedural and operational responsibilities, not financial exposure, and is an essential component of PG’s authority to manage the litigation.

The level of control that Gramercy has sought to exercise over these documents  which govern solicitor-client relationships, not funder obligations  goes far beyond the usual parameters of a lender–borrower relationship. It represents an overreach into the
 conduct and management of the litigation itself, rather than oversight of financial risk. That distinction is fundamental, and Gramercy’s continued involvement in these matters strays beyond what is permissible for a funder maintaining a proper arm’s-length
 relationship with the litigation.

It therefore appears that our collective position is that PG is now openly operating in a world where the funder of the firm has direct management/control of aspects of the litigation - and that control is on-going, despite representations to the contrary made
 to the Court, the Defendants and to the staff. This creates significant issues for the staff working on these Litigations both in our duties to our clients and to the clients of the other firms in our firm's role as Lead Solicitors. 




Can you please advise on the following:





why representations have been made to the Court, Defendants and staff that Gramercy do not have any role in the conduct, control or management of the NOx Group Litigations when plainly - they do and continue
 to do so;

whether the Board intends to update the Court as to the true position; and

whether the Board intends to inform the clients and other claimant firms of Gramercy's input into documents that have a direct bearing on costs and client instructions.





We are continuing to consider this on-going issue as more information comes to light. All of our rights are reserved.

Dear Richard, Toby, Dinah,




First of all, very nice to meet you by e-mail -- I am happy to be taking over from Michael on the Ford claim and Quantum, and look forward to working with you!




Michael is preparing an update for you regarding the PDD Trial which will be with you tomorrow. I will also send you an update on Quantum shortly.

 that is the subject of the claim being brought in this litigation.




Consequently, we have advised Ms Bottomley that she should proceed with the claim through Baby J’s Ltd and that the claim in her personal name must be discontinued.




Before we proceed with filing the notice of discontinuance, we respectfully seek your instructions to:





Discontinue Ms Bottomley’s claim in her personal capacity in the Ford Group Litigation; and
Remove Ms Bottomley from the Ford Group Register.

As with the previous discontinuance of Kenneth Gormley’s claim, we want to clarify that this action will not have any negative impact on the litigation overall. While the Defendants will be entitled to recover certain costs due to this discontinuance, it is
 likely that on account of the Anti-Avoidance Endorsement (AAE) these costs will be paid by the ATE provider, although we suspect they will reserve their right to seek these costs either form Pogust Goodhead, or from Ms Bottomley herself. This will not result
 in any financial liability for you or the other Claimants. The costs associated with this discontinuance are expected to be minimal, particularly as Ms Bottomley's claim is part of the broader litigation and the common costs will be shared across the entire
 group.




As we proceed with this process, we do not anticipate any immediate costs being incurred, and we will continue to monitor the situation closely. If you have any questions or would like to discuss this further, I am available to do so.




We kindly request your instructions to proceed with the discontinuance of Ms Bottomley's claim, as outlined above.




Kind regards,

Dear Richard, Toby and Dinah,

 

I hope you are all well. We have finished the first week of trial on Ford and I have set out an update below. Greg Lewis, a partner at PG who is in copy,
 will write to you separately about quantum related matters.  As you will be aware from my update on 7 October 2025, I am leaving Pogust Goodhead and
Greg will also have conduct of this matter going forward.




Executive Summary




Overall, the Claimant team is content with how things have gone. You may recall I previously flagged certain potential issues with our mechanical expert
 prior to the trial. I am pleased to report that these concerns did not manifest themselves significantly to the detriment of the case. Mr Carder performed reasonably well under cross examination, provided balanced and well reasoned answers to questions put
 to him by the Defendants, and engaged in good spirits with the Judge, who appeared to very much enjoy his candour. 




Day one and two 




We opened with the Ben Jaffey KC and Tom de la Mare KC on behalf of the Claimants' cross examining Dr Marcus Davies, a calibration manager who has worked
 at Ford for the past 25+ years. 




Mr Jaffey took Mr Davies through his career at Ford before putting documents to him about how Ford calibrated their vehicles, including their deployment
 of the various Engine Control Systems ("ECS") including EGR, LNT and SCR. He also put various points to Dr Davies on what "reduction in effectiveness" actually means in real world. 




Dr Davies' evidence showed that:

1) Ford knew what had to be done to their vehicles to
 pass the regulatory test, the New European Driving Cycle ("NEDC"); and

2) Ford programmed or calibrated their vehicles to do that and little else more.




Dr Davies did not dispute this and in fact, agreed with it. When he was asked to explain why Ford later updated their vehicles to be able to perform to
 a standard that was better than just the narrow confines of the NEDC, and without changing any of the hardware in the vehicles, his answers were less than convincing. There was a dichotomy in his evidence: he suggested that Ford took years to develop engines,
 with extensive testing to establish the limits of the components to which the vehicles were calibrated but then Ford was able to update and expand the calibration of the vehicles, without changing any hardware. For example, Dr Davies was taken to documents
 showing that as far back as 2012, Ford was working to improve its EGR rates, but there was limited reason as to why they didn't implement this prior to selling the vehicles. 




Tuesday morning focus moved to two further key areas: the 6th gear issue in the Transit van, and DeSOx:

1) Dr Davies was taken to documents that shows that certain Ford Transits, when using 6th gear, as indicated by the Gear Shift Indicator, increase their
 output NOx level by over 130%. Dr Davies did not seem surprised by this. 

2) Similarly, he seemed unbothered by the DeSOx documents that were put to him. DeSOx is the terminology used to describe an issue which affects certain
 Ford vehicles with an LNT whereby the LNT catalyst becomes saturated with SOx (another noxious gas) such that it cannot effectively act to reduce NOx. Once the LNT is compromised by SOx, the vehicle spews out NOx at vast rates and so they must purge the LNT
 of SOx, by performing what are known as "DeSOx events" to cleanse the catalyst. This comes at a significant cost of fuel economy for which consumers have to pay. The Claimants' application to amend the pleadings remains outstanding, and this is due to be heard
 next year.




The Claimant team consider that nothing in Dr Davies' evidence immediately helped Ford's position. In certain respects, it assisted our case, including
 as regards updates and proof that Ford could have improved their vehicles earlier; instead Ford primarily focused on other issues such as cost and fuel economy as opposed to regulatory compliance and environmental issues. 




On day two, the Claimant software expert, Dr Markus Heitz then took the stand. As with the September hearing, the Defendants sought to criticise Dr Heitz's
 report that it duplicated work in the Mechanical expert report, and that it was beyond his remit of instruction. Dr Heitz performed well under cross examination. Ultimately, however, much of the software analysis was agreed between the experts and Dr Heitz's
 cross-examination was quite short. 




Day three and four




Day three opened with the Defendants cross examination of the Claimants' mechanical expert, Mr Dan Carder. Despite our reservations about Mr Carder, he equipped himself well over the course of the cross examination. 




The Defendants' counsel team, consisting of Neil Moody KC and Sonia Nolten KC, took turns to cross examine Mr Carder, with Ms Nolten cross examining him on SCR and other available alternative technology, while Mr Moody covered "everything else". The Defendants'
 cross examination seemed relatively light touch and they did not go into depth on much of Mr Carder's report. 




Mr Carder dealt with their questions well and enjoyed good humour with the Judge, Lady Justice Cockerill.  He came across genuine and authentic (which has been our experience of him) and the Defendants failed to probe Mr Carder on a number of tricky areas arising
 out of his report. 




Mr Moody took Mr Carder through general points of principle and his analysis of the testing results. Mr Carder rightly pointed out that he was only there to present the data and make general points about what the Defendants could have done, at one point observing
 that it was not for him to "design a new and compliant Ford vehicle for them".  There were some comments made by Mr Carder that were not ideal, including his stating that "less EGR does not necessarily mean more NOx" but this was anticipated by us as being
 an opinion that he would share and so we were unsurprised. 




Ms Nolten then took Mr Carder through the SCR technology, an area that the Claimants' case is not as strong on as other points. She made a number of observations and suggestions that Mr Carder agreed with which may be less helpful as we move into closing submissions.
 He ultimately did not agree with her suggestion that the modulation that Ford deployed was suitable  - a key point in our argument that Ford did not calibrate their vehicles appropriately. Ms Nolten also cross-examined Mr Carder about alternative technologies.
 Mr Carder performed well. 




The morning of day four had Ms Nolten finish her questioning on SCR and then move onto alternative technology, an area that Mr Carder performed well in. While he did not make any positive assertions about what alternative
 technology "Ford should" have been using in their vehicles, he was firm that "Ford
could" have been using alternative (and we say better) technology in their vehicles.
 The Defendants' line of questioning on this at times seemed to suggest that Ford should not be held to the same standard as other manufacturers who were deploying better technology, and we think the Judge took note of
 this. Mr Carder asked the same question of Ms Nolten as to "do you think that Ford couldn't do it if VW could" who declined to answer the question. 




He made a number of good points back to the Defendants in cross examination and, most importantly, the Defendants failed to interrogate him on a number of salient areas of his report which now means they go unchallenged and are accepted in evidence, which is
 important for the case. 




Our junior barrister, Ms Joanna Buckley, lead the cross examination of Prof Migliorero, the Defendants' software expert. Similar to Dr Heitz, given much of the evidence was agreed, his cross examination was relatively short, however Ms Buckley managed to get
 a number of key admissions and agreements out of Prof Migliorero, which are salient for the overall case, and important for the cross examination of Ford's mechanical expert, Professor Frederico Millo, which commences on Monday. 




It transpires that Prof Migliorero is a former student of Prof Millo and they have worked together closely over the years. Ms Buckley, in cross examination, put to Prof Migliorero that certain paragraphs in his and Prof Millo's reports were identical. Prof Migliorero
 confirmed that the wording was from his report, and it was in fact, incorrect, which we imagine will make for a mildly embarrassing position for Prof Millo come Monday when his examination commences. 




Ms Buckley elicited from Prof Migliorero that software updates and the expansion of how the ECS operates were done within the constraints of the existing hardware but the main piece was that he confirmed the reports were prepared in concert. 




Summary




We are 4 days through 6.5 days of evidence on Ford, and so far, it appears that the wind is blowing in our favour. The Judge will take her own view on the evidence and submissions, and we still have to hear evidence on PCD, Renault and Nissan, but it seems
 to be a case of "so far, largely so good". 




I will send you a further update on Wednesday to confirm how the cross-examination of Prof Millo has gone, and Greg will write to you separately about quantum trial matters.  




Kind regards,




Michael & the Ford Litigation Team

We expect that the Defendant team will try to concentrate on Mr Carder. We have identified a number of likely topics that they will focus on when in cross-examination including some
 of the views he expressed in the Joint Statement on de-rating of various components of the vehicles and public literature regarding this. They may also delve into previous publications he has released in the United States on the available technology for controlling
 and regulating NOx emissions. Mr Carder is as well prepared as he can be for these topics and we remain confident in his ability to navigate any,
tricky questions, ultimately however there will inevitably be points that the Defendant team will be able to make some headway. On the flip side of this, in our preparation for the cross-examination of Professor Migliorero and Millo, our counsel team
 have identified significant discrepancies in their evidence, and what we have uncovered in disclosure and through testing as to undermine their opinions. Similarly, when considering their evidence as against the witness statements of Dr Davies (who has worked
 at Ford for in excess of 20 years), we have identified some key areas of disagreement to probe them on.

Week 3 and 4: Mercedes




Following the previous updates, please see below update regarding the Mercedes portion of the trial which ran from 29 October until 6 November. 




There is significant correlation between Ford and Mercedes, as indeed there is across each of the 5 lead manufacturers, in that the technology that each manufacturer used is broadly similar i.e. they all used one of, or a combination of, the following types
 of technology; exhaust gas re-circulation ("EGR"), Lean NOx Traps ("LNT"), selective catalytic reduction ("SCR") and diesel particular filter ("DPF"). Each manufacturer used these technologies and strategies to varying degrees and
 in different ways with different calibrations and to differing levels of success. This in itself is helpful for our claim as their arguments and the reality of how they used the technology variously cut across each other as to the component limits or availability
 of technology at the time of use (some of the defences advanced by the Defendants).  It also helps us show that there was fundamental and systemic deliberate behaviour to pass laboratory tests at the expense of real-world driving compliance, despite the protestations
 of the Defendants. 




Week 3: Mercedes Mechanical Engineering Evidence (29-30 October) 

The third week focused on the Claimants' and Mercedes’ mechanical engineering evidence concerning the principal emissions control technologies installed in its cars to control the levels of NOx . These are EGR and SCR, which reduces NOx levels by converting
 it into water and nitrogen. The Claimants' mechanical engineering expert, Mr Juston Smithers was cross examined by counsel for Mercedes. We consider that he did well and withstood three days of cross-examination in a professional and knowledgeable way. 

Since Mercedes did not call factual witnesses, the examinations concerned expert evidence only. This, in our opinion and in our submissions to the Court, is quite illuminating.


Claimants’ Expert: 



Mr Juston Smithers (the Claimants' mechanical expert) demonstrated that EGR was programmed to operate at a higher rate during test conditions (and thus meet the emissions limits), with EGR downrating (performing to a significantly lower effectiveness level)
 outside of test conditions leading to higher NOx. 


Mr Smithers explained that Mercedes’ SCR system showed reduced effectiveness during extended idling or stop-start driving, causing elevated NOx in urban conditions, outside the levels permitted under the regulations. 


He argued that Mercedes’ safety justifications were speculative and unsupported. 





Mercedes’ cross-examination of Mr Smithers: 



Ms Helen Davies KC (the barrister for Mercedes) challenged Mr Smithers’ qualifications and data analysis. 


She claimed that any EGR downgrading was due to safety and ammonia slip concerns, which Mr Smithers disputed and which he advised were unsupported by contemporaneous documents. Such concerns, he said, would not justify Mercedes’ calibration choices such that
 the calibration choices were not immediately lead by these concerns but were instead likely lead by other considerations such as production cost.   


Mr Smithers was questioned about his analysis of NOx levels before and after Mercedes’ software updates, which showed large unexplained differences in emission levels. He concluded these variations were linked to changes in Mercedes’ calibration strategy, rather
 than random variation. 


 

Week 4: Mercedes Software and Mechanical Engineering Evidence (3-6 November)  

Week four saw further cross-examination of the Claimants' experts, Dr Heitz (software engineering who is the same expert in Mercedes and Ford, as he is for all of the cases for the Claimants) and Mr Smithers and of the Defendants’ expert witnesses, Dr John
 Martens (software engineering) and Raoul Spencer Day (mechanical engineering).

The Claimants' counsel team focused on the internal engineering and software design choices within Mercedes-Benz vehicles, arguing these revealed deliberate calibration to pass laboratory tests at the expense of real-world compliance. The Defendants’ experts
 on the other hand maintained that the systems reflected legitimate engineering trade-offs, a similar argument to that which For dare attempting to advance.    

Claimants’ Experts: 



Dr Heitz and Mr Smithers confirmed that Mercedes’ SCR system used different dosing modes in tests and in real driving conditions, with higher AdBlue dosing — and therefore lower NOx — only under test conditions.   


The Claimants' experts’ position was that Mercedes’ firmware and calibration choices aligned with test-cycle boundaries (notably the NEDC 20–30°C temperature range) and that NOx emissions rose sharply just outside these parameters. This confirmed “cycle recognition”
 behaviour. 


Defendants’ Experts: 



Dr John Martens & Raoul Spencer Day (Ricardo plc) were challenged over their objectivity as experts in this litigation, given their extensive work for car manufacturers and commercial ties to several Defendants. They confirmed such relationships.   


Mr Day accepted that Portable Emissions Measurement Systems (“PEMS”) could have been used to calibrate vehicles for real-world driving but were not, and conceded that Mercedes’ firmware initially switched off NOx controls at altitude — this was later
 corrected by software updates.  


He accepted that US models used more effective emission hardware, with EU models prioritising fuel economy instead. This is positive for Ford given this is a tenet of our allegations against Ford.



Mercedes insisted these differences reflected regional regulations and safety trade-offs, not cheating, and claimed the Emissions Regulation applied mainly to type-approval tests rather than real-world conditions.

Dear Anna, 



Thank you for your email. 



We have some overarching points to raise before addressing the points in your email regarding the Side Letter Agency Agreement (“SL AA”). 



First and foremost, we have raised serious and significant issues regarding how traumatic we, and the entire team, are finding this process and that we have genuine concerns for
 the mental health and well-being of our staff. We further flagged that the proposal creates a two-tier structure amongst the wider team, which risks alienating individual members of the staff. Your email worryingly does not address any of those concerns, nor
 does it even mention them. 



We also note that various junior staff within the NOx department have been enlisted to send out correspondence, including on weekends, relating to non-common work and non-PDD
 Trial matters (see, for example, an email from Hannah Varghese at 15.32 on Saturday, 4 October 2025). Requiring the most junior staff to become actively involved in non-common work issues, while on the other hand attempting to assert that “everything we
 have done or are intending to do is with the best interests of our clients as well as our staff in mind first and foremost” is simply unreal. Correspondence of that nature and related to non-common work should be sent by an individual not working on critical
 workstreams.  



Each of the case leads are committed to finding a co-operative solution to the issues that are being raised. That is why we are proactively engaging in discussions and, in aid
 of assisting the firm, why we have continued to raise points so as to avoid the firm falling foul of issues that they may otherwise be presented with, e.g. noting potential additional disclosure obligations re. documents referred to in witness statements.
 You also have said that you “welcome any specific input we wish to contribute”. This is difficult to contemplate as being a genuine offer in circumstances where a) the SL AA was provided by Leigh Day (“LD”), not you nor the Board, despite Pogust
 Goodhead (“PG”) being our employer; and b) where we have previously sought to provide input (e.g. meeting with Alicia Alinia at 18:00 Monday 29 September 2025) and you have not engaged with it. Instead, you have sent us an email that dismisses our concerns
 and informs us that our description of the SL AA is incorrect, while at the same time stating that your intention is for this email to now bring these discussions to a conclusion. This is neither helpful nor is it in the spirit of co-operation.  



For the avoidance of any doubt, we do not consent to the SL AA in its current form. No representations can be made to the Court at the PTR on 6 October that this has been put
 in place and is agreed. To the extent that you and the Board believe you can bind individuals named in the SL AA (or annexes) by virtue of it being a ‘firm decision’ we disagree for reasons set out below. Every individual subject to the agreement either does
 not consent to it (the case leads) or, as far as we are aware, has never seen any version of it and so is unable to have provided consent.  We accept of course, that Counsel can inform the Court (on 6 October or otherwise) that it is being drafted and the
 intention is that it will be put in place in due course.  



If we, as the collective case leads, are to work collaboratively with the Board and you, and HR, to establish how we can move forward amicably, then it requires serious engagement
 from you and the Board, and not a dismissal of our concerns.  



We trust that this email will allow for a more collaborative approach going forward. 



On the points in your email: 


1.                  
Purpose and Effect of the Side Letter 


You explained that PG’s proposed role is intended to operate “exactly as envisaged”
within the existing Pan-NOx AA framework, and that the SL AA will simply implement a delegation of common work from LD to PG personnel. If that were indeed the case, a separate SL AA would not be necessary; indeed, this accords with our own understanding
 that the new arrangement is entirely novel.  



 



You say this agreement is to “ensure that [we] can continue to work as currently on the existing work plans.” Having reviewed the SL AA, it is clear that it goes
 further than the delegation provisions in the Pan-NOx AA, and that is precisely why it requires a standalone agreement. The SL AA imposes materially different terms in at least two key respects: 



 



a.
Formal separation of supervision and control 



The SL AA introduces an unusual structure whereby PG personnel will perform common work solely under the direction of LD, but remain employed and supervised by PG. Indeed, we
 understand that the Board intends for PG personnel to carry out generic/firm-specific work under PG’s direction. This formalises a split between line management and professional control that is not addressed, let alone authorised, in the Pan-NOx AA. That agreement
 permits delegation of work to another firm, not delegation of the supervision of one firm’s employees to another while the employer retains all employment obligations. 



 



b.
Governance over PG’s internal personnel decisions 



The SL AA (via Annex B) requires LD’s consultation and agreement before PG can add or remove PG personnel from common work. That means PG cannot unilaterally deploy or reassign
 its own staff in this litigation without LD’s approval. This imposes external governance over PG’s workforce, a control that is not contemplated in the Pan-NOx AA and which cuts across PG’s autonomy as an employer. 



 



The SL AA changes the status quo in material ways such that it cannot be said that what is being proposed is “exactly what we have all been working under” or that “this will not
 practically change much day to day.”  



 


2.                  
Tension with Employment Contracts 


Because the SL AA goes beyond what is authorised in the Pan-NOx AA, it creates direct tension with the terms of PG employment contracts. You advise that “there will be no change
 to your employment contract” and that “consent by employees is not necessary for PG to execute the agency agreement.” We respectfully disagree. 



Clause 2(b) of the SL AA states that “PG Personnel shall perform such Common Work … solely under the direction of, and reporting solely to, Leigh Day.” This directly conflicts
 with multiple provisions that we presume appear in each individual employee contract: 


 

a.
Duty of obedience and supervision 

Under Clause 4/Duties of the employment contract (which we presume is a standard term of contract for all PG employees), PG employees are contractually required to comply with
 PG’s directions and report to PG line managers. They are to “devote the whole of their time, attention and abilities to the business of the Company.” The SL AA seeks to override that by imposing a structure in which we report solely to LD in respect
 of a major portion of our work, without any formal secondment or variation of contract. 

 

b.
Regulatory oversight 

The split between day-to-day supervision (by LD) and formal employment responsibility (by PG) creates regulatory ambiguity under the SRA Code of Conduct. Who is the supervising
 solicitor? Are there two supervising solicitors, one from Leigh Day and another from PG? Which firm bears responsibility for ensuring compliance with professional standards?  

 

These are not academic questions - they carry regulatory and indemnity implications.  

 

c. Consent and legal clarity 

The arrangement introduces a dual-control model, but without staff consent, proper transparency, or any framework setting out lines of accountability. As PG remains the employer,
 yet LD directs our work in practice, the legal and ethical basis for this arrangement is unclear, particularly when conflicts, confidentiality obligations, or errors arise. 


 


3.                  
Professional Indemnity Insurance Risk 
The SL AA structure also raises serious questions around insurance cover. If PG personnel are performing common work
 solely under LD’s direction (as the SL AA confirms), then it is not clear whose professional indemnity (“PI”) insurance would respond in the event of a professional error. This is in circumstances where PG remains the/our employer and is responsible
 for holding PI cover for its staff. But LD is envisaged as exercising the day to-day control and making the litigation decisions. The SRA expects supervision and insurance liability to be aligned. That is not the case here. 


 



This is not hypothetical. A clear example of this risk occurred this week when LD made a costs offer to the Mercedes Defendants without PG’s knowledge or approval from PG's insurer
 - despite the fact that PG personnel had prepared the underlying work. If that offer proves problematic, it is unclear whether PG or LD (or both) would be liable and, more importantly,
whose insurer would be on risk. That ambiguity creates risk for both firms and undermines the clarity of the delegation framework set out in the Pan-NOx AA. 



 



This is precisely why the Pan-NOx AA structured delegation at the firm level: to avoid splitting supervision and risk in a way that confuses accountability. The SL AA unpicks
 that structure and introduces unnecessary exposure. 



 



We refer you to 17(a) of the PTR skeleton argument filed by Mercedes where the Defendants have drawn the Court’s attention to this issue. 



 


4.                  
Client Consent 


If PG wishes for us and other PG staff to be instructed by, and report solely to, a firm other than PG, then this requires our express consent, and (we believe) the informed consent
 of the clients whom we act on behalf of (which will not only be just the clients of PG, but  may extent to all clients within every GLO if the work is to be Pan-NOx). If PG personnel are to carry out work on those clients’ cases under the direction of a different
 firm, the clients must be told who is supervising that work and must provide informed instructions to that effect. We refer you to Rule 1.4 of the Code of Conduct, which requires solicitors to ensure clients are in a position to make informed decisions about
 their representation. You cannot unilaterally impose this on us, or on any of the PG staff, nor PG’s clients as your email  suggests you can. 
 
You cannot unilaterally impose a change of supervisory firm on your employees or on the clients, as your email equally suggests. The assumption that this arrangement can simply be implemented without individual or client-level engagement is not supported by
 the regulatory framework. This concern is not novel: post our comments in this regard, this is also expressly identified in the skeleton argument filed by Mercedes at paragraph 17(b), where they raise the potential for regulatory impropriety in precisely these
 circumstances. 



Turning to other points specifically raised in your email:  


·               
You note that we are obliged to work our notice periods. Thank you for pointing this out again, although we note it is not consistent with representations that PG has made
 to the Defendants and Court that the timing of our last days are subject to ongoing discussion. You go on to say that once our notice period has expired, we are free to commence working for JLG, should we so choose. Collectively, none of us have informed you
 of our plans post-PG.  

 

·               
You have advised that LD and counsel have approved this solution. Please provide us with this correspondence (including the advice the firm has taken from counsel –
 as originally requested). We note that as per Martyn Day’s email on 3 October at 13.56 that “Alicia has asked that we leave these issues for PG to sort out with the team. We await the outcome of those discussions and so no need for the meeting this afternoon.”
 In circumstances where LD are waiting for PG to “sort out these issues with the team” and that they will “await the outcome”, we fail to understand how LD have approved the solution. 

 

·               
You advise that you are “now interviewing so with time this work-stream will be handed over”. Please explain which work-stream? Does this relate to non-common work? 


We repeat that we are keen to try and work together to find a collaborative solution to these issues, not least because of the importance of the upcoming PDD Trial beginning in
 a little over a week’s time and for which we are all deeply invested in and, in truth, where all of this is causing a huge and detrimental distraction. However, it is plain to us that the SL AA is plainly more than a simple delegation mechanism. It alters
 the control and supervision structure, restricts PG’s governance over its own staff, creates clear tension with employment contracts and regulatory obligations, and places work done on behalf of the PG clients under the instruction of an external law firm
 (without any proposal for client consent to be obtained). If there is to be a material change, it needs to be handled transparently and within a proper legal framework. We raise these points constructively and in good faith, with the shared goal of ensuring
 compliance and continuing to act in our clients’ best interests.
